solution:
A species is diamagnetic only when every electron is paired, i.e. when the number of unpaired electrons \(n = 0\). Writing the outer configuration of each ion and counting unpaired 3d electrons (Table 8.7):

\(\mathrm{Cr^{2\oplus}} = 3d^4\) — 4 unpaired, paramagnetic.

\(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}} = 3d^5\) — 5 unpaired, paramagnetic.

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}} = 3d^9\) — 1 unpaired, paramagnetic.

\(\mathrm{Sc^{3\oplus}} = 3d^0\) — scandium is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^1\ 4s^2}\), so losing three electrons empties both the 4s and the 3d orbitals and leaves the bare argon core. With no unpaired electrons at all, \(\mu = 0\) and the ion is repelled by a magnetic field.

Only \(\mathrm{Sc^{3\oplus}}\) has \(n = 0\), so it is the diamagnetic one.

Titanium is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^2\ 4s^2}\) and Table 8.3 lists its oxidation states as \(+2, +3, +4\).

\(+5\) is not available at all — titanium has only four electrons outside the argon core, so it cannot reach \(+5\); that option can be rejected outright.

Of the three states it does show, \(+2\) (\(3d^2\)) and \(+3\) (\(3d^1\)) both leave electrons in the 3d subshell and are readily oxidised further. In the \(+4\) state titanium has lost both 4s and both 3d electrons and is left with the \(3d^0\) argon core — a completely empty d subshell, which the chapter identifies as an especially stable arrangement.

Hence \(+4\) is the most stable oxidation state of titanium, as in \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\) and in the colourless \(\mathrm{Ti^{4\oplus}}\) ion of Table 8.8.

[Textbook misprint: the printed question reads "Components of Nichrome alloy are are" — the word "are" is set twice across the line break on printed page 190. Nothing has been lost; the stem is transcribed exactly as printed.]

The chapter's list of uses of alloys states it directly: "Nichrome an alloy of nickel and chromium in the ratio 80 : 20 has been developed specifically for gas turbine engines." So nichrome is a two-component alloy of nickel and chromium.

The options adding iron, or iron and carbon, describe the ferrous alloys of the same section (nickel steel, chromium steel, stainless steel), where iron is the major constituent — nichrome is not one of these. Copper and iron together are not a nichrome composition at all; the chapter's copper alloys are bronze (copper and tin), brass (copper and zinc) and cupra-nickel (copper and nickel).

Hence the components are Ni and Cr.

The question asks for the most STABLE oxidation state, which is not the same as the highest one.

The chapter notes that third-series elements reach \(+8\), "as in \(\mathrm{(RuO_4)}\) and \(\mathrm{(OsO_4)}\)". That makes \(+8\) the highest state ruthenium attains, but \(\mathrm{RuO_4}\) is a volatile, powerfully oxidising compound that decomposes readily — it is the least stable of the states listed, not the most stable, so \(+8\) is rejected.

\(+2\) is a low state for a heavier transition metal; the chapter's own point is that the second and third rows stabilise HIGHER oxidation states than the 3d row does, so \(+2\) is not where ruthenium's stable chemistry lies. \(+6\) (for example the ruthenate ion) is again strongly oxidising and reverts to lower states.

Ruthenium's stable, ordinary chemistry is that of Ru(IV) — for instance \(\mathrm{RuO_2}\), which is a stable solid. Hence \(+4\).

Chromium is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^5\ 4s^1}\) and Table 8.3 lists its oxidation states as \(+2\) to \(+6\).

In \(+3\) the ion is \(3d^3\); this is the state chromium ends up in whenever it is reduced, and the chapter's dichromate reactions all finish at chromic sulphate \(\mathrm{Cr_2(SO_4)_3}\), i.e. Cr(III). In \(+6\) chromium has given up all six of its \(3d^5 4s^1\) electrons; this is the state of the two commercially important salts the chapter devotes §8.7 to, \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\) and \(\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\), both stable isolable solids.

The other pairs each contain a state that chromium shows only as a transient intermediate: \(+2\) is strongly reducing and is rapidly oxidised to \(+3\), and \(+4\) and \(+5\) appear in Table 8.3 but have no stable, isolable compounds in this chapter.

Hence the stable pair is \(+3, +6\).

Table 8.2 gives the OBSERVED ground-state configuration of copper as \(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^{10}\ 4s^1}\), not the expected \(3d^9 4s^2\); the chapter explains this as the extra stability of a completely filled 3d subshell. So the neutral atom is \(3d^{10}, 4s^1\), which at once eliminates the options beginning \(3d^9, 4s^1\) and \(3d^8, 4s^1\).

Ionisation removes the outermost, highest-energy electron first, which here is the single 4s electron. Table 8.4 confirms this: the \(\mathrm{M^{\oplus}}\) row for copper reads \(3d^{10}\ 4s^0\). So \(\mathrm{Cu^{\oplus}}\) keeps its full \(3d^{10}\) shell and has an empty 4s orbital, which also eliminates the remaining option, whose ion is written \(3d^9, 4s^0\).

Hence Cu is \(\mathrm{3d^{10}, 4s^1}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu^{\oplus}}\) is \(\mathrm{3d^{10}, 4s^0}\).

A \(\mathrm{d^0 s^0}\) ion is one that has lost every electron outside the preceding noble-gas core. Test each ion against the neutral configurations of Table 8.2:

Sc is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^1\ 4s^2}\) — three electrons outside argon, so \(\mathrm{Sc^{3\oplus}}\) is \(3d^0 4s^0\). Table 8.8 lists it as \(3d^0\).

Ti is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^2\ 4s^2}\) — four outside argon, so \(\mathrm{Ti^{4\oplus}}\) is \(3d^0 4s^0\). Table 8.8 lists it as \(3d^0\).

V is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^3\ 4s^2}\) — five outside argon, so \(\mathrm{V^{5\oplus}}\) is \(3d^0 4s^0\).

All three qualify, so no single-ion option can be the answer and the correct choice is "all of the above". This is also why exercise question 2 (iii) can ask why the salts of these very three ions are colourless: with no d electrons there can be no d-d transition.

The spin-only formula of §8.6.4 is \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\) BM, where \(n\) is the number of unpaired electrons. Evaluating it for each option:

\(n = 2\): \(\sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8} = 2.83\) BM.

\(n = 3\): \(\sqrt{3 \times 5} = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\) BM.

\(n = 4\): \(\sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\) BM.

\(n = 5\): \(\sqrt{5 \times 7} = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\) BM.

Only the last matches the measured 5.9 B.M.; the next nearest value, 4.90 BM, is a whole Bohr magneton away, so the identification is unambiguous. Table 8.7 gives the same figure for the \(3d^5\) ions \(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}\).

Hence the complex has 5 unpaired electrons.

§8.14 says of the actinoid series: "Most of these elements are not found in nature. They are all radioactive and man-made." That is an unqualified statement about every member of the series, so the actinoids are the set required.

The lanthanoids are explicitly excluded by §8.12 (iv): "Except promethium (Pm), all are non-radioactive in nature" — one radioactive member does not make the series radioactive.

The d-block elements of the chapter — the 3d, 4d and 5d series it tabulates — are ordinary stable metals such as iron, copper and silver, and the s-block contains sodium, potassium and calcium; neither series is radioactive throughout.

Hence only the actinoids.

A \(\mathrm{Ln^{3\oplus}}\) ion is paramagnetic only if it has at least one unpaired 4f electron. Table 8.13 gives the number of unpaired electrons directly:

\(\mathrm{La^{3\oplus}}\) is \(4f^0\) with 0 unpaired electrons and an observed moment of 0 — diamagnetic.

\(\mathrm{Lu^{3\oplus}}\) is \(4f^{14}\) with 0 unpaired electrons and an observed moment of 0 — diamagnetic.

Every set containing either of these therefore fails: the first set contains \(\mathrm{Lu^{3\oplus}}\), and the second and third both contain \(\mathrm{La^{3\oplus}}\).

The remaining set is \(\mathrm{Ce^{3\oplus}}\) (\(4f^1\), 1 unpaired), \(\mathrm{Eu^{3\oplus}}\) (\(4f^6\), 6 unpaired) and \(\mathrm{Yb^{3\oplus}}\) (\(4f^{13}\), 1 unpaired) — all three have unpaired f electrons and non-zero observed moments (2.3-2.5, 3.3-3.5 and 4.3-4.9 BM), so all three are paramagnetic.

§8.14 answers this in its own words: "The half-lives of the isotopes of thorium (Th-232 = \(1.4 \times 10^{10}\) years) and uranium (U-238 = \(4.5 \times 10^{9}\) years) are so long that these elements exist in rocks on earth."

Thorium is therefore the actinoid, other than uranium, that survives in significant amount in the earth's crust — its half-life is longer even than uranium's and comparable with the age of the earth. §8.16 adds that this is why thorium(IV) oxide could be used in everyday gas mantles.

Actinium and protactinium are named nowhere as naturally abundant; they occur only in trace amounts as short-lived members of the uranium and thorium decay chains. Plutonium is one of the man-made elements of §8.14 and is produced in nuclear reactors, not mined.

Hence thorium.

A flux is the substance added to the charge to combine with the gangue and carry it off as a fusible slag. §8.9.2 says of the blast furnace: "Limestone acts as flux, it combines with the gangue material to form molten slag", and the zone-of-slag-formation reactions show how: \(\mathrm{CaCO_3 \longrightarrow CaO + CO_2}\), then \(\mathrm{CaO + SiO_2 \longrightarrow CaSiO_3}\). Limestone is calcium carbonate.

Silica and alumina are rejected because the chapter names them as the GANGUE itself — "The gangue contains silica, alumina and phosphates" — that is, the impurities the flux is added to remove, not the flux.

Sodium carbonate is a flux in a different process altogether: §8.7.4 uses anhydrous \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) when roasting chromite ore, not in the extraction of iron from haematite.

Hence calcium carbonate.
